results.prompt: Build a loan calculator with a slider for the amount.
results.raw:
Here's a live loan calculator — drag the amount slider (and the rate/term) and the monthly payment, total interest and cost split update instantly.

:::intelligent-ui{v="1"}
root = Stack([grid1, sec1, card1])
grid1 = Grid([m1, m2, m3])
m1 = Metric("Monthly payment", monthly, "Annuity loan: principal + interest", "positive")
m2 = Metric("Total interest", interest, "Over the full term", "warning")
m3 = Metric("Total cost", totalcost, "Principal + interest")
sec1 = Section("Your loan", [s1, s2, s3, row1])
s1 = Slider("Loan amount (kr)", $amount, 100000, 5000000, 50000)
s2 = Slider("Interest rate (%)", $rate, 1, 15, 0.1)
s3 = Slider("Term (years)", $years, 1, 30, 1)
row1 = Row([b1, b2, b3])
b1 = Button("1 500 000 kr", @Set($amount, 1500000))
b2 = Button("3 000 000 kr", @Set($amount, 3000000))
b3 = Button("Reset", @Reset($amount))
card1 = Card("Where the money goes", [ch1])
ch1 = Chart("donut", "Principal vs interest (kr)", ["Principal", "Interest"], [{name: "kr", values: [$amount, interest]}])
$amount = 1500000
$rate = 5.5
$years = 20
r = $rate / 1200
n = $years * 12
g = (1 + r) ^ n
monthly = $amount * r * g / (g - 1)
totalcost = monthly * n
interest = totalcost - $amount
:::

The term is the lever most people underestimate: stretching the loan lowers the monthly payment noticeably, but total interest grows since you pay interest for more years. If you can afford it, a shorter term plus extra down payment cuts the total cost fastest; a rate change of one percentage point typically moves the monthly payment by several hundred kroner on a loan this size.

Here's an interactive mortgage calculator — drag the sliders and the payment, totals and split update instantly.

:::intelligent-ui{v="1"}
root = Stack([form1, grid1, card1, card2])
$loan = 3000000
$rate = 5
$years = 25
r = $rate / 1200
n = $years * 12
monthly = $loan * r / (1 - (1 + r) ^ (0 - n))
totalPaid = monthly * n
totalInterest = totalPaid - $loan
pay15 = $loan * r / (1 - (1 + r) ^ (0 - 180))
pay20 = $loan * r / (1 - (1 + r) ^ (0 - 240))
pay25 = $loan * r / (1 - (1 + r) ^ (0 - 300))
pay30 = $loan * r / (1 - (1 + r) ^ (0 - 360))
form1 = Form("Mortgage details", [f1, f2, f3])
f1 = Field("Loan amount", [sl1])
sl1 = Slider("Amount", $loan, 500000, 10000000, 50000)
f2 = Field("Interest rate", [sl2], "Annual nominal rate")
sl2 = Slider("Rate (%)", $rate, 0.5, 10, 0.1)
f3 = Field("Term", [sl3], "Number of years to repay")
sl3 = Slider("Years", $years, 5, 35, 5)
grid1 = Grid([m1, m2, m3])
m1 = Metric("Monthly payment", monthly, "Principal + interest")
m2 = Metric("Total interest", totalInterest, "Over the full term", "warning")
m3 = Metric("Total cost", totalPaid, "Principal + interest", "neutral")
card1 = Card("Where the money goes", [ch1])
ch1 = Chart("donut", "", ["Principal", "Interest"], [{name:"Total cost", values:[$loan, totalInterest]}])
card2 = Card("Same loan, different terms", [tbl1])
tbl1 = Table("", ["Term", "Monthly payment", "Total interest"], [["15 years", pay15, pay15 * 180 - $loan], ["20 years", pay20, pay20 * 240 - $loan], ["25 years", pay25, pay25 * 300 - $loan], ["30 years", pay30, pay30 * 360 - $loan]])
:::

Amounts are in your own currency unit. Notice the trade-off in the table and the donut: stretching the term shrinks the monthly payment but the interest slice grows faster than the principal shrinks — so the cheapest loan overall is the shortest term you can comfortably afford, while the lowest monthly cost sits at the longest.

Here's an interactive BMI calculator — drag the sliders and the BMI, category and scale update instantly.

:::intelligent-ui{v="1"}
root = Stack([g1, m1, r1, ch1])
$h = 175
$kg = 75
g1 = Grid([sH, sW])
sH = Slider("Height (cm)", $h, 140, 210)
sW = Slider("Weight (kg)", $kg, 35, 160)
m1 = Metric("Your BMI", bmi, category, tone)
r1 = Row([bH, bW])
bH = Button("Reset height", @Reset($h))
bW = Button("Reset weight", @Reset($kg))

category = bmi < 18.5 ? "Underweight" : (bmi < 25 ? "Normal weight" : (bmi < 30 ? "Overweight" : "Obese"))

BMI is a rough screening tool only: it doesn't distinguish muscle from fat, so athletes often read "overweight", and it says nothing about where fat sits. For a real picture, pair it with waist circumference and body-fat percentage.

results.prompt: Build a savings calculator with a monthly deposit slider.

results.raw:
Here's a three-mode percentage calculator — slide the values and the results update instantly.

:::intelligent-ui{v="1"}
root = Tabs([tab1, tab2, tab3])
tab1 = Tab("X% of Y", [s1, s2, presetRow, m1])
tab2 = Tab("X is what % of Y", [s3, s4, m2])
tab3 = Tab("Percent change", [s5, s6, m3, b3])
s1 = Slider("Percent", $pct, 0, 100, 1)
s2 = Slider("Value (Y)", $val, 0, 1000, 5)
presetRow = Row([p10, p20, p25])
p10 = Button("10%", @Set($pct, 10))
p20 = Button("20%", @Set($pct, 20))
p25 = Button("25%", @Set($pct, 25))
m1 = Metric("Result", ofResult, "X% of Y")
ofResult = $pct * $val / 100
s3 = Slider("Part (X)", $part, 0, 500, 1)
s4 = Slider("Whole (Y)", $whole, 1, 500, 1)
m2 = Metric("Result", shareResult, "X as a percent of Y")
shareResult = $part / $whole * 100
s5 = Slider("From", $from, 1, 1000, 5)
s6 = Slider("To", $to, 0, 1000, 5)
m3 = Metric("Change", changeResult, "Positive = increase, negative = decrease")
changeResult = ($to - $from) / $from * 100
b3 = Badge($to >= $from ? "Increase" : "Decrease", $to >= $from ? "positive" : "warning")
$pct = 15
$val = 200
$part = 30
$whole = 150
$from = 120
$to = 150
:::

Three things are worth noting: the first tab answers "how much is a percentage of a number" (15% of 200 = 30), the second converts a part into a percentage (30 of 150 = 20%), and the third measures growth between two numbers (120 → 150 = +25%). Switch tabs at the top to change mode; the presets in the first tab are handy for tips or VAT.

Here's a live converter — pick a tab, choose units, and type any amount:

:::intelligent-ui{v="1"}
root = Stack([i1, tabs])
$val = "1"
$lenFrom = "Meter"
$lenTo = "Kilometer"
$wtFrom = "Kilogram"
$wtTo = "Pound"
$volFrom = "Liter"
$volTo = "Gallon (US)"
$tempFrom = "Celsius"
$tempTo = "Fahrenheit"
i1 = Input("Value to convert", $val, "e.g. 12.5")
tabs = Tabs([t1, t2, t3, t4])
t1 = Tab("Length", [r1, m1])
r1 = Row([s1, s2])
s1 = Select("From", $lenFrom, unitsLen)
s2 = Select("To", $lenTo, unitsLen)
unitsLen = ["Meter", "Kilometer", "Centimeter", "Mile", "Foot", "Inch"]
m1 = Metric("Converted length", resLen, "Same distance, other unit")
resLen = $val * fLen / tLen
fLen = $lenFrom == "Kilometer" ? 1000 : $lenFrom == "Centimeter" ? 0.01 : $lenFrom == "Mile" ? 1609.344 : $lenFrom == "Foot" ? 0.3048 : $lenFrom == "Inch" ? 0.0254 : 1
tLen = $lenTo == "Kilometer" ? 1000 : $lenTo == "Centimeter" ? 0.01 : $lenTo == "Mile" ? 1609.344 : $lenTo == "Foot" ? 0.3048 : $lenTo == "Inch" ? 0.0254 : 1
t2 = Tab("Weight", [r2, m2])
r2 = Row([s3, s4])
s3 = Select("From", $wtFrom, unitsWt)
s4 = Select("To", $wtTo, unitsWt)
unitsWt = ["Kilogram", "Gram", "Pound", "Ounce", "Tonne"]
m2 = Metric("Converted weight", resWt, "Mass is preserved")
resWt = $val * fWt / tWt
fWt = $wtFrom == "Gram" ? 0.001 : $wtFrom == "Pound" ? 0.45359237 : $wtFrom == "Ounce" ? 0.028349523 : $wtFrom == "Tonne" ? 1000 : 1
tWt = $wtTo == "Gram" ? 0.001 : $wtTo == "Pound" ? 0.45359237 : $wtTo == "Ounce" ? 0.028349523 : $wtTo == "Tonne" ? 1000 : 1
t3 = Tab("Volume", [r3, m3])
r3 = Row([s5, s6])
s5 = Select("From", $volFrom, unitsVol)
s6 = Select("To", $volTo, unitsVol)
unitsVol = ["Liter", "Milliliter", "Gallon (US)", "Cup", "Cubic meter"]
m3 = Metric("Converted volume", resVol, "Liquid or dry capacity")
resVol = $val * fVol / tVol
fVol = $volFrom == "Milliliter" ? 0.001 : $volFrom == "Gallon (US)" ? 3.785411784 : $volFrom == "Cup" ? 0.2365882365 : $volFrom == "Cubic meter" ? 1000 : 1
tVol = $volTo == "Milliliter" ? 0.001 : $volTo == "Gallon (US)" ? 3.785411784 : $volTo == "Cup" ? 0.2365882365 : $volTo == "Cubic meter" ? 1000 : 1
t4 = Tab("Temperature", [r4, m4])
r4 = Row([s7, s8])
s7 = Select("From", $tempFrom, unitsTemp)
s8 = Select("To", $tempTo, unitsTemp)
unitsTemp = ["Celsius", "Fahrenheit", "Kelvin"]
m4 = Metric("Converted temperature", resTemp, "Offsets applied, not just a factor")
cTemp = $tempFrom == "Fahrenheit" ? ($val - 32) * 5 / 9 : $tempFrom == "Kelvin" ? $val - 273.15 : $val
resTemp = $tempTo == "Fahrenheit" ? cTemp * 9 / 5 + 32 : $tempTo == "Kelvin" ? cTemp + 273.15 : cTemp
:::

Two things worth knowing: the value you type is shared across all four tabs, so you can switch category without retyping it — and temperature is handled with offsets rather than a single multiplication factor, which is why it lives in its own tab.

Annual billing simply charges for 10 months instead of 12 — at 25 seats on Pro that's 14 750 USD instead of 17 700 USD, so the switch is where the real saving lives. The bar chart scales linearly with seat count, so the gap between tiers grows as the team gets bigger; Basic only wins if seats stay small and you don't need SSO or audit logs.

results.raw:
Here's a representative 12-month revenue picture (no figures were supplied, so these are illustrative placeholders — swap in your real numbers and the shape of the story stays the same):

:::intelligent-ui{v="1"}
root = Stack([g1, c1])
g1 = Grid([m1, m2, m3])
m1 = Metric("Latest month", "1.31M kr", "1.31M Dec vs 0.98M a year earlier", "positive")

m3 = Metric("Avg. monthly growth", "+4.4%", "Compounding through the year", "positive")
c1 = Card("Monthly revenue (thousands kr)", [ch1])
ch1 = Chart("line", "", ["Jan","Feb","Mar","Apr","May","Jun","Jul","Aug","Sep","Oct","Nov","Dec"], [{name:"This year", values:[820,865,910,880,940,1010,990,1050,1120,1180,1240,1310]}, {name:"Last year", values:[700,720,760,790,810,830,850,870,890,920,950,980]}])
:::

**What it means**

- **The trend is up, and steadily so.** Revenue rose every month except two small dips (April and July), and the annual total is roughly a fifth higher than last year. That's growth, not just noise.
- **The gap to last year is widening.** The two lines start close together and fan apart toward year-end. The current period isn't only ahead — it's accelerating, which usually means the growth is compounding rather than a one-off spike.
- **Watch the two flat months (Apr, Jul).** Mild dips are normal, but if they repeat in the same months next year it's probably seasonality; if they spread, it's worth checking pricing, churn or a sales-capacity limit.
- **The run-rate matters more than any single month.** December alone is 1.31M; annualised, that's a pace of ~15.7M versus the 12.3M actually booked. The difference tells you how much growth is still "in the pipeline" if the recent pace holds.

**So what?** If you're planning headcount, spend or targets, the safest assumption is that the year-end run-rate — not the yearly average — is your new baseline.

results.prompt: Compare React vs Vue vs Svelte.
Which is better for a startup, Stripe or Adyen?
results.raw:
Short answer: for almost every startup in the first few years, **Stripe**. Adyen wins later, once payments volume is large enough that interchange++ savings and direct acquiring outweigh the extra engineering and contracting overhead.

:::intelligent-ui{v="1"}
root = Stack([cmp, tbl, d1])
cmp = Comparison("Stripe vs Adyen for a startup", [stripe, adyen])
stripe = {name: "Stripe", attributes: ["Live in minutes — no sales call or contract", "Flat rate, e.g. ~2.9% + 30c per card charge", "No monthly fee, no volume minimum", "Best-in-class docs, SDKs, hosted checkout", "Billing, invoicing, subscriptions, tax included", "Payouts in ~2 business days (varies by country)"]}
adyen = {name: "Adyen", attributes: ["Onboarding is sales-led and takes weeks", "Interchange++ pricing — cheaper at real volume", "No monthly fee, but contract and volume expectations", "You build more yourself: checkout, risk, tokenization", "Direct acquiring + local methods in many markets", "Best for high volume, multi-currency, and in-person"]}
d1 = Divider()
tbl = Table("Where they actually differ", ["Dimension", "Stripe", "Adyen"], [["Time to first payment", "Minutes to days", "Weeks (contract + review)"], ["Pricing model", "Flat % + fixed fee", "Interchange++ (cost + markup)"], ["Cheapest when", "Low/medium volume", "High volume, optimized routing"], ["Engineering effort", "Low — use their stack", "High — bring payments in-house"], ["Support", "Self-serve, docs-first", "Account/enterprise tiered"], ["Best fit stage", "Pre-seed to Series A/B", "Scale-ups and enterprise"]])
:::

**Practical rule of thumb:** start on Stripe, revisit around the point where payment fees are a meaningful line item — roughly several million in annual processed volume, or when a large share of revenue comes from non-card, non-US, or in-person payments. At that point Adyen's interchange++ model and direct acquiring can cut effective cost enough to justify the migration, and the sales team will actually take the call.

Two caveats worth knowing: Adyen typically doesn't court very small merchants, so applying too early can just stall you; and the headline fee difference often shrinks once you account for the engineering time to rebuild checkout, retries, and reconciliation. Many scale-ups end up running Stripe for speed and Adyen (or a similar acquirer) for cost — routing volume between them rather than picking one forever.

You didn't name the tiers, so here's a representative two-tier comparison using typical SaaS values — tell me your actual numbers and I'll swap them in.

:::intelligent-ui{v="1"}
root = Stack([c1, d1, b1])
c1 = Comparison("Subscription tiers", [{name:"Basic",attributes:["$9 / month","1 user seat","5 GB storage","Community support","Core features only","No API access"]},{name:"Pro",attributes:["$29 / month","5 user seats","100 GB storage","Priority email support","Advanced analytics + integrations","Full API access"]}])
d1 = Divider()
b1 = Badge("Pro is the better fit once you need more than one user or API access", "positive")
:::

The decision usually hinges on two things: how many people need access, and whether you need the API. Below 2 users with no integration work, Basic is the cheaper path. Once you're past that, Pro's price gap is typically recovered by the extra seats alone.
